subproblem.title: Countable open cover with Lipschitz pieces for a map locally Lipschitz on an arbitrary set (parent step 1)
subproblem.statement: For all P, Q ∈ ℕ, every set U ⊆ ℝ^P and every map f : ℝ^P → ℝ^Q that is locally Lipschitz on U, there are open sets O_i ⊆ ℝ^P and constants K_i ∈ ℝ≥0 (i ∈ ℕ) such that U ⊆ ⋃_i O_i and f is K_i-Lipschitz on O_i ∩ U for every i. Here 'locally Lipschitz on U' means: every x ∈ U has a neighbourhood t within U (t ∈ 𝓝[U] x) and a constant K ≥ 0 such that f is K-Lipschitz on t.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P Q : ℕ) (U : Set (Eucl P)) (f : Eucl P → Eucl Q), LocallyLipschitzOn U f → ∃ (O : ℕ → Set (Eucl P)) (K : ℕ → ℝ≥0), (∀ i, IsOpen (O i)) ∧ U ⊆ ⋃ i, O i ∧ ∀ i, LipschitzOnWith (K i) f (O i ∩ U)
subproblem.natural_proof:
Conventions. ℝ^P = Eucl P = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin P). `LocallyLipschitzOn U f` means: for every x ∈ U there are K ∈ ℝ≥0 and a set t ∈ 𝓝[U] x (a neighbourhood of x within U) such that f is K-Lipschitz on t (`LipschitzOnWith K f t`: edist (f y) (f z) ≤ K · edist y z for all y, z ∈ t). Being K-Lipschitz on a set passes to its subsets (`LipschitzOnWith.mono`), and every map is 0-Lipschitz on ∅ (`lipschitzOnWith_empty`).

1. (Local open pieces.) Fix x ∈ U and choose K_x ∈ ℝ≥0 and t_x ∈ 𝓝[U] x with f K_x-Lipschitz on t_x. A set belongs to 𝓝[U] x iff it contains O ∩ U for some open O ∋ x (Mathlib `mem_nhdsWithin`). So there is an open O_x ⊆ ℝ^P with x ∈ O_x and O_x ∩ U ⊆ t_x, and f is K_x-Lipschitz on O_x ∩ U by monotonicity. (For x ∉ U put O_x := ∅ and K_x := 0, so x ↦ O_x is a total function. These values are never used: the Lindelöf step below only involves O_x for x ∈ U, and every point it returns lies in U.)

2. (Lindelöf.) ℝ^P is second countable, hence hereditarily Lindelöf, so every subset of ℝ^P, in particular U, is Lindelöf (Mathlib instance `SecondCountableTopology.toHereditarilyLindelof`, lemma `HereditarilyLindelofSpace.isLindelof U`). For x ∈ U the open set O_x contains x, so O_x ∈ 𝓝 x. The neighbourhood form of the Lindelöf property (Mathlib `IsLindelof.elim_nhds_subcover`; equivalently, the open cover {O_x : x ∈ U} of U has a countable subcover) gives a countable set T ⊆ U with U ⊆ ⋃_{x ∈ T} O_x.

3. (Case T = ∅.) Then U ⊆ ⋃_{x ∈ ∅} O_x = ∅, so U = ∅. Take O_i := ∅ and K_i := 0 for every i ∈ ℕ. Each O_i is open, U = ∅ ⊆ ⋃_i O_i, and f is 0-Lipschitz on O_i ∩ U = ∅.

4. (Case T ≠ ∅.) A nonempty countable set is the range of a sequence (Mathlib `Set.Countable.exists_eq_range`), so T = {g(i) : i ∈ ℕ} for some g : ℕ → ℝ^P. Put O_i := O_{g(i)} and K_i := K_{g(i)}. Since g(i) ∈ T ⊆ U, step 1 shows that O_i is open and f is K_i-Lipschitz on O_i ∩ U for every i.

5. (Cover.) Let x ∈ U. By step 2 there is y ∈ T with x ∈ O_y, and y = g(i) for some i ∈ ℕ, so x ∈ O_{g(i)} = O_i. Hence U ⊆ ⋃_i O_i. Together with step 4 (or step 3 when T = ∅) this proves the claim. ∎
proof_key_steps: For each x ∈ U choose K_x and an open O_x ∋ x with O_x ∩ U ⊆ t_x (mem_nhdsWithin), so f is K_x-Lipschitz on O_x ∩ U.
ℝ^P is second countable, hence hereditarily Lindelöf, so some countable T ⊆ U has U ⊆ ⋃_{x∈T} O_x.
If T = ∅ then U = ∅, and O_i = ∅, K_i = 0 work.
Otherwise T = range g; put O_i := O_{g(i)} (open) and K_i := K_{g(i)}. Then f is K_i-Lipschitz on O_i ∩ U and U ⊆ ⋃_i O_i.

audit.reason: The prose and exact Lean proposition match, with arbitrary U and nonnegative Lipschitz constants. Relative neighborhoods yield the required open pieces; hereditary Lindelöfness gives a countable subcover. The proof correctly handles an empty index set and enumerates a nonempty countable set. Openness supports the parent's continuity argument. Every step is justified without relying on this child, its sibling, or the parent theorem.

subproblem.title: Compact inner approximation of σ-finite null-measurable sets in ℝ^P (parent step 3)
subproblem.statement: For every P ∈ ℕ, every measure μ on the Borel σ-algebra of ℝ^P, and every μ-null-measurable set A ⊆ ℝ^P such that the restriction μ⌞A is σ-finite, there are compact sets C_k ⊆ A (k ∈ ℕ) with μ(A ∖ ⋃_k C_k) = 0.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P : ℕ) (μ : Measure (Eucl P)) (A : Set (Eucl P)), NullMeasurableSet A μ → SigmaFinite (μ.restrict A) → ∃ C : ℕ → Set (Eucl P), (∀ k, IsCompact (C k)) ∧ (∀ k, C k ⊆ A) ∧ μ (A \ ⋃ k, C k) = 0
subproblem.natural_proof:
Conventions. ℝ^P = Eucl P carries its Borel σ-algebra, μ is any measure on it, and μ⌞A = `μ.restrict A`. For a Borel set B, μ⌞B(E) = μ(E ∩ B) for every E ⊆ ℝ^P (Mathlib `Measure.restrict_apply'`); for a Borel set E, μ⌞A(E) = μ(E ∩ A) for every A (`Measure.restrict_apply`). 'μ-null-measurable' means measurable for the completion of μ (`NullMeasurableSet A μ`).

1. (Borel kernel.) Since A is μ-null-measurable, there is a Borel set A′ ⊆ A with A′ = A μ-almost everywhere (Mathlib `NullMeasurableSet.exists_measurable_subset_ae_eq`). In particular μ(A ∖ A′) = 0.

2. (Finite pieces.) Since μ⌞A is σ-finite, there are Borel sets S_m (m ∈ ℕ) with ⋃_m S_m = ℝ^P and μ⌞A(S_m) < ∞ for every m (Mathlib `spanningSets (μ.restrict A)` with `measurableSet_spanningSets`, `measure_spanningSets_lt_top`, `iUnion_spanningSets`). Put B_m := A′ ∩ S_m; it is a Borel set. Since B_m ⊆ A′ ⊆ A, we have B_m ∩ A = B_m, hence μ(B_m) = μ(B_m ∩ A) = μ⌞A(B_m) ≤ μ⌞A(S_m) < ∞.

3. (Inner regularity on one finite piece.) Fix m and put ν_m := μ⌞B_m, so ν_m(E) = μ(E ∩ B_m) for every E. Then ν_m(ℝ^P) = μ(B_m) < ∞, so ν_m is a finite Borel measure on ℝ^P. Since ℝ^P is a σ-compact metric space, every locally finite (in particular every finite) Borel measure on ℝ^P is regular (Mathlib `Measure.Regular.of_sigmaCompactSpace_of_isLocallyFiniteMeasure`; classically Simon Ch. 1, Theorem 1.15(2) with Remarks 1.16 and 1.12, or Ulam's tightness theorem for finite Borel measures on Polish spaces). In particular ν_m is inner regular with respect to compact sets on Borel sets of finite measure (Mathlib: `Regular` gives `InnerRegularCompactLTTop`, and then `MeasurableSet.exists_isCompact_sdiff_lt`, whose remaining hypotheses hold because ℝ^P is Hausdorff and its Borel σ-algebra contains the open sets). Applying this to the Borel set B_m, which has ν_m(B_m) = μ(B_m) < ∞, gives for every j ∈ ℕ a compact set K_{m,j} ⊆ B_m with ν_m(B_m ∖ K_{m,j}) < 1/(j+1). As B_m ∖ K_{m,j} ⊆ B_m, ν_m(B_m ∖ K_{m,j}) = μ((B_m ∖ K_{m,j}) ∩ B_m) = μ(B_m ∖ K_{m,j}). Hence μ(B_m ∖ K_{m,j}) < 1/(j+1) for all m, j ∈ ℕ.

4. (Null remainder in each piece.) Fix m. For every j, B_m ∖ ⋃_{j′} K_{m,j′} ⊆ B_m ∖ K_{m,j}, so by monotonicity and step 3, μ(B_m ∖ ⋃_{j′} K_{m,j′}) < 1/(j+1). Letting j → ∞ gives μ(B_m ∖ ⋃_{j′} K_{m,j′}) = 0.

5. (Global remainder.) Let x ∈ A ∖ ⋃_{m,j} K_{m,j}. If x ∉ A′, then x ∈ A ∖ A′. If x ∈ A′, choose m with x ∈ S_m (the S_m cover ℝ^P); then x ∈ B_m and x ∉ ⋃_j K_{m,j}, so x ∈ B_m ∖ ⋃_j K_{m,j}. Hence A ∖ ⋃_{m,j} K_{m,j} ⊆ (A ∖ A′) ∪ ⋃_m (B_m ∖ ⋃_j K_{m,j}). By monotonicity and countable subadditivity, together with steps 1 and 4, μ(A ∖ ⋃_{m,j} K_{m,j}) = 0.

6. (Re-indexing.) Let k ↦ (a(k), b(k)) := Nat.unpair k, a surjection ℕ → ℕ × ℕ because Nat.unpair (Nat.pair m j) = (m, j). Put C_k := K_{a(k), b(k)}. Each C_k is compact, and C_k ⊆ B_{a(k)} ⊆ A′ ⊆ A. By surjectivity, ⋃_k C_k = ⋃_{m,j} K_{m,j}. Step 5 then gives μ(A ∖ ⋃_k C_k) = 0. ∎
proof_key_steps: Choose a Borel A′ ⊆ A with A′ = A μ-a.e., so μ(A ∖ A′) = 0.
σ-finiteness of μ⌞A gives Borel S_m covering ℝ^P with μ(A′ ∩ S_m) = μ⌞A(A′ ∩ S_m) < ∞.
The finite Borel measure μ⌞(A′ ∩ S_m) on the σ-compact metric space ℝ^P is regular. This gives compact K_{m,j} ⊆ A′ ∩ S_m with μ((A′ ∩ S_m) ∖ K_{m,j}) < 1/(j+1).
Hence μ((A′ ∩ S_m) ∖ ⋃_j K_{m,j}) = 0. Since A ∖ ⋃_{m,j} K_{m,j} ⊆ (A ∖ A′) ∪ ⋃_m ((A′ ∩ S_m) ∖ ⋃_j K_{m,j}), subadditivity makes it μ-null.
Re-index K_{m,j} by ℕ via Nat.unpair to get compact C_k ⊆ A with μ(A ∖ ⋃_k C_k) = 0.

audit.reason: The prose and exact Lean proposition match, including the Euclidean Borel measurable structure, null measurability, and sigma-finiteness of the restriction only. The measurable kernel and spanning sets produce finite Borel pieces. Their finite restricted measures satisfy the required regularity assumptions, yielding compact subsets with errors tending to zero. The remainder inclusion, countable null union, and Nat.unpair reindexing establish exactly the conclusion. No global regularity or sigma-finiteness of μ is assumed, and the supplied proof is complete and non-circular.
